topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: LiteLLM Router
description: LiteLLM Router (litellm.Router, BerriAI; open-source Python SDK + Proxy/AI-Gateway) is the most-adopted real-world LLM routing layer: a unified OpenAI-compatible interface to 100+ LLM providers with load balancing, fallbacks, retries, cooldowns, timeouts, cost tracking, caching, guardrails, and observability. It is an operational/infrastructure router — it distributes requests for a logical model name across many deployments using configurable strategies (simple-shuffle, least-busy, usage-based-routing v1/v2, latency-based-routing, cost-based-routing) and fails over across deployments and model groups. It does NOT decompose prompts, plan multi-agent topologies, or do semantic/intent-based skill routing; its 'routing' is deployment selection for reliability, cost, and throughput. Included here for the adoption and routing_layer dimensions: ~33K-40K GitHub stars, 470K+ proxy downloads, production use at Netflix, Lemonade, and Rocket Money.
decomposition_method: None — LiteLLM Router does not decompose prompts. A request for a logical model name is passed through whole; there is no splitting into sub-tasks, parsing, or clustering. Routing operates at the deployment-selection level, not the intent level. [uncertain]
decomposition_granularity: Not applicable — the unit is a single API request (one completion/embedding call); no sub-task granularity exists. [uncertain]
ordering_strategy: Not applicable to sub-tasks. The only ordering concept is deployment priority via the 'order' field in litellm_params (lower = higher priority; order=1 tried before order=2, etc.) and accumulated fallback hops — i.e., ordering of retry/failover targets, not ordering of decomposed sub-tasks. [uncertain]
decomposition_validation: Not applicable — there is no decomposition step to validate. The closest analog is health/cooldown checks that exclude failing deployments from selection, but no solvability/completeness/non-redundancy verification of any task split. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat — a single request mapped to one deployment from a model group; no milestone/step hierarchy or skill tree. (Settings do resolve hierarchically Keys > Teams > Global, but that is config precedence, not task hierarchy.) [uncertain]
router_type: rule-based / policy-driven deployment selector (not a classifier over intents). It picks a deployment within a model group by the configured routing_strategy (simple-shuffle weighted by rpm/tpm, least-busy, usage-based v1/v2, latency-based, cost-based) plus retries and fallback chains. No single/multi-label intent classification, graph planning, or retrieve-then-rerank.
routing_model: rule-based / heuristic — selection is driven by configuration and runtime metrics (rpm/tpm weights, current load, observed latency, cost, cooldown state), not by a learned model, embeddings, or an LLM. No ML router is involved in standard operation.
handles_ambiguity: Not applicable to intent ambiguity — there is no semantic disambiguation. For operational 'which deployment' choices among equivalent peers, it uses the routing strategy (e.g., weighted random / least-busy); it never asks the user, abstains, or reasons about intent. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: Robust operational fallback (a core feature): on a retryable failure it retries within the same model group (optionally enable_weighted_failover re-picks a different deployment by weight before escalating), then falls back to other model groups via configured fallback chains (e.g., {'gpt-3.5-turbo': ['gpt-4']}), including context_window_fallbacks for context-length errors and client-side fallbacks. Failing deployment IDs are excluded and exclusions accumulate across hops. This is failover between deployments/models, not re-decomposition or human escalation.
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: Scales to 100+ providers / many deployments per model group via full-config enumeration — all deployments and model groups are declared in config; selection is by routing strategy over the group, not by embedding retrieval or rerank. The 'pool' is model deployments, not a skill/tool registry, so retrieve-then-rerank and skill-tree traversal do not apply. [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Not applicable — there is no skill body vs. name+description distinction; the router selects among model deployments described by static config (model name, rpm/tpm, cost, region), not skills with hidden bodies. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: Single-call pass-through with retry/fallback wrapping. Architecturally the router wraps a request in try/except, delegates to function_with_retries (its own try/except + in-group retries), which calls the unified litellm.completion/embeddings function; on failure it retries/falls back. No fan-out, DAG, or multi-tool execution per request. [uncertain]
parallel_vs_concurrent: Not applicable to a single request (sequential pass-through with retries). LiteLLM does support high-throughput concurrent handling of many independent requests and batching features at the gateway level, but it does not parallelize sub-tasks of one prompt. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: Not applicable — no sub-tasks, so no inter-sub-task dependency analysis. [uncertain]
result_aggregation: Not applicable — one request yields one response; there is no merging of multiple sub-results. (The gateway aggregates logs/spend/metrics, but not task outputs.) [uncertain]
mid_chain_feedback: Not applicable — single-shot request with retries; no multi-step plan to re-route. Runtime feedback exists only as cooldown/health signals that influence the next independent request's deployment choice. [uncertain]
benchmark_name: None — not a research system; no accuracy benchmark. It is evaluated operationally (throughput, latency, reliability) in load tests rather than on task-accuracy benchmarks. [uncertain]
multi_intent_coverage: Not applicable — no notion of compound/multi-intent prompts; routing is per-request deployment selection. [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: Not applicable — no routing-correctness/accuracy metric. Operational metrics (success rate, latency, cost, throughput) are tracked instead of tool-name or AST accuracy. [uncertain]
clarification_capability: Not measured / not supported — no clarification behavior. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: Not applicable — no decomposition to score on process vs. outcome. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Not applicable to task-accuracy reproducibility. Reliability is engineered via retries/fallbacks/cooldowns; throughput results from LiteLLM's own load tests (e.g., simple-shuffle with rpm/tpm maximized throughput) are environment-dependent, not a standardized benchmark. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: standalone service (Proxy Server / AI Gateway) OR in-process SDK (litellm.Router) — deploy the proxy as a centralized gateway for routing/retries/fallbacks/auth/spend across providers, or embed the Router class directly in a Python app. It is middleware between the application and the LLM providers, not a LangGraph node or inference-engine extension.
routing_layer: application-layer / gateway (proxy or SDK) — it sits above the model providers as an AI gateway; it is NOT inference-engine-layer routing (no Envoy/ext_proc/vLLM-internal classification). A recent sidecar architecture reduces proxy overhead but remains an app-tier gateway.
latency_overhead: Low for routing itself (simple-shuffle is the recommended production default for minimal overhead); the gateway adds a network hop and bookkeeping. No decomposition step, so no pre-execution token/round-trip cost. Note Python concurrency limits at extreme scale (alternatives like Go-based Bifrost claim far lower per-request latency at very high RPS).
online_adaptation: Runtime-adaptive heuristics, not learned. It continuously adapts deployment selection to live signals (rpm/tpm usage, latency, cost, cooldowns/health) so traffic shifts away from degraded/expensive deployments, but there is no RL/bandit policy learning or fine-tuning from feedback — selection rules are static config; only the metrics they consume update. [uncertain]
adoption: Production deployment + open-source (most-adopted real-world routing layer): open-source at github.com/BerriAI/litellm (~33K-40K stars), 470K+ proxy downloads, 100+ providers, used in production by Netflix, Lemonade, and Rocket Money; ships virtual keys, spend tracking, guardrails, load balancing, admin dashboard, MCP support, and an Agent Hub. The de facto integration/reliability layer rather than a semantic intent router.
